qt: to the Commission Stelios Kouloglou (The Left) Subject:

There is increasing concern about the serious bout of African swine fever (ASF) that has recently hit the EU and specifically Greece and Bulgaria1. ASF was recently detected in wild boar in most of North Greece23, especially in areas near the Bulgarian border, signalling a potential risk of cross-border contamination. Meanwhile, Bulgaria has reported a wave of ASF cases both in wild boar and domestic pig populations. Not only do these cases threaten the livelihoods of local livestock farmers, they pose a serious risk to the EU’s entire agricultural sector, potentially harming food security and economic stability. The impact on pig farming is catastrophic, especially for the indigenous Greek black pig, an ancient species that is part of local cultural heritage. In view of this: Given how fast ASF is spreading and the serious impact it is having on the livestock population, could the Commission specify what measures it intends to put in place to prevent the disease from spreading further within the EU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Stelios Kouloglou (The Left) (25 April 2024) Subject: Measures to alleviate plight of African swine fever in Greece and Bulgaria and measures to curb spread of this zoonotic disease There is increasing concern about the serious bout of African swine fever (ASF) that has recently hit the EU and specifically Greece and Bulgaria (1). ASF was recently detected in wild boar in most of North Greece (2) (3), especially in areas near the Bulgarian border, signalling a potential risk of cross-border contamination. Meanwhile, Bulgaria has reported a wave of ASF cases both in wild boar and domestic pig populations. Not only do these cases threaten the livelihoods of local livestock farmers, they pose a serious risk to the EU’s entire agricultural sector, potentially harming food security and economic stability. The impact on pig farming is catastrophic, especially for the indigenous Greek black pig, an ancient species that is part of local cultural heritage. In view of this: Given how fast ASF is spreading and the serious impact it is having on the livestock population, could the Commission specify what measures it intends to put in place to prevent the disease from spreading further within the EU? (11 June 2024) Since the start of the African swine fever (ASF) epidemic in Europe in 2007, the Commission took a series of initiative s (4) to address a possible incursion of the disease into the EU. Since the first occurrence of ASF in the EU in 2014, the Commission took a great number of measures (5) to prevent, control and eradicate it. The Commission is closely monitoring the ASF epidemiological situation in Bulgaria and Greece, providing political, technical, and financial support to control and eradicate this devastating disease. A major EU instrument to manage ASF is regionalisation. The Commission adopts ASF regionalisation measures based on EU legislation with a science-based approach. These measures allowed the Commission to manage the spread of ASF and contributed to the eradication of ASF in Czechia, Belgium and from certain zones of Germany. This tool also provides solid guarantees to other Member States and trading partners. Other targeted tools deployed by the Commission to support Bulgaria and Greece is the EU Veterinary Emergency Team deployed within a few days to provide immediate support to affected Member States with tailor made advice, and ad hoc trainings, such as the Sustained Training Missions, to help Member States to develop control action plans for the medium-long term. The EU also provides co-financing to Member States for certain control measures to prevent, control and eradicate ASF with the use of two instruments, namely the Union veterinary programmes (6) and the Union contribution to emergency measures (7).
